section: Legislative procedure - ordinary, money, financial and constitutional amendment bills; joint sitting
subsections: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case
Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent

accepted.s: Which one of the following is included within the scope of a Money Bill under Article 110(1) of the Constitution?
o: Fees for licences issued by local authorities
Taxes imposed by a municipality for local purposes
Imposition of fines by a criminal court
Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax
accepted.x: A Money Bill may deal with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax. Fines, licence fees and local taxes are not, by themselves, matters of a Money Bill.
accepted.tq: Identify the exact constitutional subject instead of selecting nearby revenue-related terms.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT a matter specified in Article 110(1) as relating to a Money Bill?
o: Appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India
Borrowing of money by the Government of India
Custody of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Contingency Fund of India
Regulation of fees for services rendered by a local authority
accepted.x: Article 110(1) covers borrowing, custody and appropriation of specified public funds, among other matters. Regulation of fees for local-authority services is not a Money Bill matter.
accepted.tq: Find the option that falls outside the specifically enumerated constitutional subjects.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Money Bill:
1. It may deal with the custody of money in the Public Account of India.
2. It may provide for the receipt of money into, or the audit of, the Consolidated Fund of India.
3. It may deal with matters incidental to the matters specified in Article 110(1).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements describe matters covered by Article 110(1), including Public Account custody, receipt or audit of Consolidated Fund money, and incidental matters.
accepted.tq: Check each statement against the constitutional list and use the comprehensive option only when every item fits.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A Bill containing provisions exclusively relating to the matters specified in Article 110(1) can be introduced in Parliament only when which one of the following conditions is satisfied?
o: It is introduced in the Lok Sabha by a private member after prior approval of the Rajya Sabha
It is introduced in the Lok Sabha by a minister on the recommendation of the President
It is introduced in either House by any member with the consent of the Speaker
It is introduced in the Rajya Sabha by a minister on the recommendation of the President
accepted.x: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, only by a minister, and only on the President's recommendation.
accepted.tq: Split the conditions by asking who introduces, where it is introduced and whose recommendation is required.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Who certifies that a Bill is a Money Bill?
o: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
accepted.x: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill. The Speaker's decision is treated as final under Article 110(3).
accepted.tq: Use the constitutional office specifically entrusted with the certification power.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
With reference to the Speaker's certificate on a Money Bill, consider the following statements:
1. The decision of the Speaker under Article 110(3) is final.
2. The certificate is endorsed on the Bill when it is sent to the Rajya Sabha.
3. The certificate is also endorsed when the Bill is presented to the President.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The Speaker's decision is final under Article 110(3), and the certificate is endorsed on the Bill sent to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.
accepted.tq: Track the certificate through both constitutional transmission stages rather than limiting it to introduction.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: If the Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within the prescribed period, the Bill is:
o: Deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form passed by the Lok Sabha
Returned to the President for reconsideration
accepted.x: When the Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form passed by the Lok Sabha.
accepted.tq: Apply the consequence of non-return instead of treating silence as rejection or deadlock.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the role of the Rajya Sabha in relation to a Money Bill?
o: It must pass the Bill without any recommendation within fourteen days.
It may return the Bill with recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject.
It may reject the Bill by a simple majority and thereby terminate it.
It may amend the Bill and its amendments are binding on the Lok Sabha.
accepted.x: The Rajya Sabha can make recommendations and return the Bill within 14 days, but the Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations.
accepted.tq: Separate the recommendatory role of the Rajya Sabha from the binding amendment power applicable to ordinary Bills.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the President's action on a Money Bill is correct?
o: The President may assent to it or withhold assent, but cannot return it for reconsideration.
The President must refer it to the Supreme Court before giving assent.
The President may return it to Parliament for reconsideration once.
The President has no constitutional role after the Speaker certifies it.
accepted.x: Under Article 111, a Money Bill cannot be returned by the President for reconsideration. The President may assent to it or withhold assent; in practice, assent follows the prior recommendation for introduction.
accepted.tq: Test the important exception that distinguishes Money Bills from ordinary Bills at the assent stage.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which case upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill, while the Money-Bill issue was subsequently referred to a larger bench in another case?
accepted.x: The Aadhaar Act was upheld as a Money Bill in K.S. Puttaswamy (2018). The Money-Bill question was later referred to a seven-judge bench in Rojer Mathew (2019).
accepted.tq: Anchor the judicial developments by matching the case names with their years and sequence.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The reference in Rojer Mathew concerning the Money-Bill issue was made to a bench consisting of:
accepted.x: In Rojer Mathew (2019), the Money-Bill question was referred to a larger seven-judge bench.
accepted.tq: Retain the exact numerical composition of the larger bench rather than relying on the usual constitutional-bench size.
accepted.sec: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A Government Bill in Parliament ordinarily requires what period of notice before introduction, whereas a Private Member's Bill requires what period?
accepted.x: A Government Bill requires seven days' notice, while a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice before introduction.
accepted.tq: Compare the two notice periods directly and watch for their reversal in the options.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the First Reading of an ordinary Bill?
o: Leave to introduce is sought, and the title and objectives are presented; it may then be published in the Gazette
The President decides whether to return the Bill for reconsideration
Clause-by-clause voting on amendments takes place
The Bill is accepted or rejected as a whole without substantive amendments
accepted.x: The First Reading concerns leave to introduce the Bill, its title and objectives, and publication in the Gazette. Clause-by-clause consideration belongs to the Second Reading, while assent is a later stage.
accepted.tq: Match the legislative action with the correct reading instead of confusing adjacent stages.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. First Reading — Publication in the Gazette
2. Second Reading — Committee stage and clause-by-clause consideration
3. Third Reading — Acceptance or rejection of the Bill as a whole
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
accepted.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. The Second Reading includes general discussion, committee consideration and clause-by-clause voting, while the Third Reading concerns the Bill as a whole.
accepted.tq: Use the stage-wise table structure to verify each pair independently.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s: During which reading of an ordinary Bill does the committee stage occur?
accepted.x: The committee stage forms part of the Second Reading, along with general discussion and consideration of the Bill clause by clause.
accepted.tq: Locate the committee stage within the sequence of readings rather than treating it as a separate reading.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Which of the following is characteristic of the Third Reading of an ordinary Bill?
1. The Bill is considered and voted upon as a whole.
2. Amendments of substance are ordinarily not made at this stage.
3. The Bill may be accepted or rejected as a whole.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
accepted.x: The Third Reading deals with the Bill as a whole; it may be accepted or rejected, and substantive amendments are not made at this stage.
accepted.tq: Combine the defining features of one stage and reject options that omit a linked feature.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s: After an ordinary Bill is passed by one House, the other House may:
o: Return it only to the President
Pass it, amend it, reject it, or keep it pending for six months
Certify it as a Money Bill
accepted.x: The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.
accepted.tq: Choose the option that lists the complete range of legislative responses rather than an exclusive power.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The absence of a constitutionally prescribed time limit for the President to act on an ordinary Bill makes possible what is commonly known as:
accepted.x: Since no fixed time limit is prescribed for presidential action, the President may keep an ordinary Bill pending indefinitely, a situation known as a pocket veto.
accepted.tq: Link the procedural omission—the absence of a time limit—with its established constitutional term.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following stages of an ordinary Bill in the correct chronological order:
A. Consideration by the second House
B. First Reading in the originating House
C. Presidential action
D. Second and Third Readings in the originating House
accepted.x: The Bill is first introduced in the originating House, undergoes its Second and Third Readings, is transmitted to the second House, and then reaches the President.
accepted.tq: Fix the first and final stages, then place the two parliamentary House stages between them.
accepted.sec: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A deadlock arising because the two Houses finally disagree on amendments to an ordinary Bill is dealt with through the mechanism provided in:
accepted.x: Article 108 provides for a joint sitting to resolve specified deadlocks between the two Houses over an ordinary Bill.
accepted.tq: Match the deadlock mechanism with the correct constitutional article, distinguishing it from Articles 109–111.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Which of the following situations can constitute a deadlock warranting consideration of a joint sitting under Article 108?
1. The other House rejects the Bill.
2. The Houses finally disagree on amendments.
3. The other House does not pass the Bill for more than six months, excluding specified periods of prorogation or adjournment.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
accepted.x: All three situations are grounds for a joint sitting. In calculating the six-month period, periods of prorogation and adjournment over four consecutive days are excluded.
accepted.tq: Test all three constitutional grounds together, including the qualifying exclusion in the time condition.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s: For the purpose of the six-month period relevant to a joint sitting, which periods are excluded?
o: Periods of prorogation and periods of adjournment over four consecutive days
All periods of parliamentary recess without exception
Only periods of dissolution of the Lok Sabha
Only periods during which the President is absent from India
accepted.x: Periods of prorogation and periods of adjournment over four consecutive days are excluded while computing the relevant six-month period.
accepted.tq: Read the time rule precisely and avoid the extreme claim that every recess is excluded.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s: If the President does not summon a joint sitting after a deadlock under Article 108, the Bill:
o: Automatically becomes law after six months
Is deemed to have been rejected by the Rajya Sabha only
Must be referred to the Supreme Court
accepted.x: If the President does not summon the joint sitting, the Bill comes to an end. It does not automatically become law or receive judicial certification.
accepted.tq: Apply the consequence of non-summoning instead of assuming that a deadlocked Bill remains permanently pending.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A decision at a joint sitting is taken by:
o: A unanimous vote of the presiding officers of both Houses
A simple majority of members present and voting in both Houses together
A special majority of the total membership of both Houses
A two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House separately
accepted.x: The Bill is decided by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting together at the joint sitting.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the voting threshold and the combined body voting from special-majority procedures.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following sets contains only the categories of Bills excluded from a joint sitting?
o: Private Members' Bills and Government Bills
Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills
accepted.x: Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills cannot be referred to a joint sitting. Financial Bills of types I and II can go to a joint sitting.
accepted.tq: Identify the two express exclusions and avoid treating every financial measure as excluded.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following statements regarding Financial Bills is correct?
o: Financial Bills of types I and II can be referred to a joint sitting.
A Financial Bill can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha.
A Financial Bill is always treated exactly like a Money Bill in the Rajya Sabha.
Both types of Financial Bills are constitutionally excluded from a joint sitting.
accepted.x: Financial Bills of types I and II can go to a joint sitting. They must not be confused with Money Bills, which are excluded from the joint-sitting procedure.
accepted.tq: Separate Financial Bills from Money Bills by testing the consequence that differs between them.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with a joint sitting of Parliament?
1. 1961 — Dowry Prohibition Bill
2. 1978 — Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill
3. 2002 — Prevention of Terrorism Bill
Select the correct answer using the code below.
accepted.x: All three pairs are correct. These are the three occasions on which a joint sitting of Parliament was held: 1961, 1978 and 2002 respectively.
accepted.tq: Verify each year–Bill pair independently, using the distinctive chronological list as the anchor.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]

accepted.s: How many joint sittings of the Indian Parliament have been held for resolving legislative deadlocks, as represented by the recorded instances of 1961, 1978 and 2002?
accepted.x: Joint sittings have been held only three times: for the Dowry Prohibition Bill, the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill.
accepted.tq: Count the complete historical list rather than inferring frequency from the constitutional provision.
accepted.sec: Joint sitting - Article 108  [APPSC]
